It gets a bit grindy mining metal from asteroids and fuel from nebulas, but you can build your own space-station and affect the state of the game-map, helping the various factions get more influence and what-not.

Anyway, it's a fun game, I like it.

A very good space simulator, with a heavy emphasis on its simulator aspects.

The game doesn't hold your hand and lets you choose how to play the game, as long as it's within the game's mechanics. Another positive feature of the game is its unforgivable nature. The main point of this game's economy and exploration imo is preplanning and analysis of what you are going to do and how you do it. Plus, the ship's customization is quite detailed, yet simple at the same time. Want better defenses?- slap some upgraded systems on (if you have enough money and hull points). Wanna haul more cargo? - add bigger cargo bays, which in early game will require you to sacrifice some other systems, like extra seats for passengers or defense / offense systems. 

Though with all of this, it may have its flaws. For some players it may be overwhelming, since it uses some of the game mechanics I haven't seen before implemented in games. One of them would be fuel economy. You have a very tight and limited fuel tank, so you need to preplan the rout and use inertia to travel with as little fuel burned as possible. There's more deep and interesting new ways of resource gathering and merchandise inside the game economy, the dev was kind enough to explain some of them on his YouTube channel (which I would recommend watching, if you wish to have an easier time with your start at playing the game or understanding some of its systems easier, and more deeply, without sitting through the tutorial). 

So overall - this game a good chilling game with unforgivable resource managment, which might not be for everyone. Lore side it might fall a bit dry, which is a good opportunity for player to create their own, if you're up for it. Treat this game as a simulator heavy experience and you'll see game shine.

This is the space game you have been waiting for.

This game is a joy to play. A joy to fly around in. With IDS switched completely off (no Flight Assist at all) it is an extremely fun challenge too. If you like Newtonian flight with NO SPEED LIMITS, 6DOF dogfighting combat, trading, mining, exploring, racing, base building and so much more, I can't explain how much fun I'm having in this game. 

One piece of advice: DO THE TRAINING. It is not too long and gets you hyped for the game, but without it, the game is too hard. Mercenary Spacecraft, prepare to launch!

EDIT after 50 hours: Oh my gosh, there is SO MUCH to this game. Not only is the flight model the best in any spaceflight simulation I've played, but there is a whole simulated economy, a galactic war and faction storylines, you can build stations and cities and set up new trade routes, explore the vast reaches of unexplored space and claim your riches, you can do all sorts of interesting varied missions which have you being everything from a delivery boy, to a combat pilot, to a bounty hunter, to a racer, to a space janitor (all where the sole focus is on flying your ship!) You can land on planets, walk around on them with a Terrain Walker vehicle. 

The other night I refuelled a stranded ship and in the distance saw beautiful lights. I flew toward them, and was engulfed in an Aurora Borealis, and flew into its centre. The Borealis interfered with my systems and I lost scanning, so I blasted up into space and into orbit, where I floated for a while as the planet beneath me turned. This is a real, living, too-scale Newtonian Universe. You can fly close to stars, and through a light-filter, see their surface. You can find wondrous things in the depths of space. 

The map system and UI are all excellent also (be careful, there's no dedicated "undock" button and you have to stay on inventory screen for tractor beam to stay attached, but it's ok to float in stations with no tractor beam, just don't do it at cities.)  You can build different ships out of different parts, even arrange the parts and paint your ship to make it truly unique, you can experiment with and modify weapons, you can space mine (most fun space mining in any game I've ever played, in fact, this is the only game I like space mining in: you have to keep your ship moving.) And you can fly in Newtonian Physics with no inertial dampening, or with plenty of computer assistance, even an autopilot! There's tons of equipment and modules for your ship, there's just so much to this game, I will be playing forever!
It's like an indie mix of Elite, X, and FreeSpace with a 90's sci-fi B movie vibe. Highly recommend it if you like space sims.

Una especie  X (me refiero a la saga de juegos,X, X2, X3, X Rebirth, X4...) pero con la posibilidad de jugar online con otros jugadores (multiplayer) en servidores publicos o privados (con gente o solo con amigos)  Al igual que en X, puedes construir tus propias estaciones e incluso ciudades, y no son simplemente algo útil para el propio jugador, sino que toda su facción (elegida al inicio, entre 2 facciones antagónicas) se beneficia de ella y le ayuda a expandirse y conquistar sectores a la facción rival.

En general puede que algo mas simple que los "X" en cuanto a la gestión macro, y mas complejo en cuanto a los detalles técnicos y pilotaje de la propia nave. No es que resulte complicado pilotar, sino simplemente que tiene muchísimos datos y detalles sobre como manejarla, como por ejemplo el desplazamiento por inercia, o un combate mas complejo donde los misiles son extremadamente letales y es necesario evadirlos usando contramedidas e incluso enfriando la nave apagando motores. Hasta que entendí ciertas cosas, mis primeros combates fueron frustrantes. Simplemente hay que cambiar el chip respecto a otros juegos y combatir de una forma mas "técnica", sin lanzarse de cabeza cargando de frente.

Mencionar también la enorme cantidad controles que ofrece. La mayoría igual son cosas que no se usan nunca, o son accesos directos a elementos que puedes acceder desde otros menús, pero la cantidad posible de controles para "automatizar" las cosas da una idea del nivel de detalle que se le ha puesto al juego. Me las he apañado para configurar controles funcionales tanto para un mando tipo Xbox como para un Hotas, pero para navegar los menús resulta mas práctico seguir usando el ratón. 

En Steam Deck funciona bien, aunque las letras son pequeñas y puede costar leer ciertas cosas. El trackpad sirve bien para hacer de ratón y usar los menús. La única pega (que quizá sea solucionable) es que la partida guardada no se sincroniza entre el Deck y el PC, pero quizá sea un error puntual o algo subsanable que no he investigado todavía.

A algunos quizá les resulte mas familiar el Elite Dangerous, en ese caso, puede decirse que es "parecido" pero mas complejo en tanto que te permite crear toda una flota a la que dar ordenes,  y ayudar a tu facción a conquistar el universo conocido (en lugar de ser un único piloto con un impacto mas bien nulo sobre el gran esquema de las cosas)

Permite entrar en cualquier planeta sin transiciones, a lo No Man´s Sky. Igualmente te permite dedicarte a lo que te de la gana: exploración, combate, compraventa de mercancias, transporte...

A destacar también la personalización de la nave. En lugar de comprar naves prediseñadas, podemos hacerlas "por piezas" e incluso esas piezas admiten cierta personalización sobre sí mismas.

En general un juego impresionante para un único desarrollador. El único punto flojo son los gráficos, algo anticuados ya, pero si puedes pasar esto por alto (tampoco son super terribles) es un sim espacial muy completo. La posibilidad de multijugador es lo que en mi opinión le falla a la serie X, y este juego cumple con ello. Igualmente, si tomamos como referencia el Elite Dangerous, este juego le añade la posibilidad de tener no solo tu nave, sino toda una flota siguiendo tus órdenes, además de permitirte construir tus propias estaciones, bases, e impactar en el universo de juego haciendo prevalecer a la facción de tu elección mediante tus acciones.

Lo recomiendo, pero ojo, no es ningún arcade, si buscas algo mas sencillo (mas arcade) recomiendo juegos como Rebel Galaxy, Everspace 2, o Starpoint Gemini 2 / Starpoint Warlords.

EvoChron Legacy Steam Review. 

First off I would have to say, I've found this game pretty addictive, racking up about 50 Hours in my first week. Not nearly enough to be an expert, but enough for a reasonably informed review. 

Richard Douglas'score is excellent and I have downloaded it and just put it on in the background with some screenshots when I am chilling out. It's really that good. 

Evochron is just amazing value for it's small file size, it competes well with much larger and more expensive offerings, like X4 quite well IMHO. I can confidently say Technical support is excellent. While I had no troubles getting the game to work on my tower; I ran into some difficulty with my laptop. Turned out that there as a small error being generated between my updated Razor Mouse Driver, and an old config file. A problem that this app was sensitive too. Anyhow it ultimately was not caused by the game, but The developer was very prompt and helpful in helping me track down the bug.

The Default Start is to begin as a Mercenary Pilot, Which I think is a left over from the games last iteration as Evochron Mercenary. As Flying and Navigating systems has some learning curve, I would suggest starting as a Miner/Trader, it will give you and opportunity to learn the controls, without being Harassed by Enemies. My current start is as an Independent, and as such I have not been attacked at all; so if your looking for a little more action you might pick Federation or Alliance; I don't think it will make any difference besides who attacks you. 

Evochron employs more keybindings than any other game I have ever played and thats a good few. Nearly every Key has a bind, and while most are just the key, a few are Alt Keyed. This is not a huge problem there is a map online that you can download and personalize; The problem is a fair number of keys can get you in a little trouble, M-Mouse Look if accidentally pressed will cut out your ability to control your spacecraft without knowing why, fortunately I found a thread addressing this problem. Obviously your going to want rebind some of these keys to a Shift or Alt, as a safety measure. I think a Gaming mouse is a huge help here too, as I personally bound my Primary Weapons to a side button on my Razor Mouse, and my left mouse button to select target in gun-site, Just a personal choice. Anyhow I think your going to want to get in a few hours flying, before your finalize your key binds. 

The Skyscapes are beautiful and the Stations and ships well executed if you love space games, you wont be bored. At the very start mining is your very best way to make money, but it soon enough will become a little tedious, so you'll want to do some trading; which while normally not nearly as profitable will get you out of the back yard. Teach you the Plotting, Hyperspace system, and allow you to check out other systems and again the game art, which very good. Landing Dirtside is a challenge the first time or two, but if you come in slow about 500Mps and follow your beacons, you'll be acing that in no time. 

Evochron is not the product of a large studio, but of one Dev. So sometimes you might have to work around a small glitch. I was running from Talison to Sapphire for the 20th time; when the pathing bugged and I kept crashing into the gateway and crashing the app. On the 4th Try I just hand flew the ship to a position directly in front of the mouth of the gate and took it through and went autopilot from there without further trouble. 10 hours Later and probably as many runs to Sapphire and have not seen the bug again. Anyhow any Indie project is going to have its needles in the haystack, but overall Evochron Legacy is more that worth them. As a long time X4 Player who just got sick to death of playing savior of the Universe and that games buggy AI; Legacy fits me like a glove, it truly is the sandbox X4 claims to be and as I am happiest in game flying about in a single seater with no one to answer to but myself. If that sounds good to you too, try this game. It does have a demo, and I'm sure you'll buy it in no time.

Summary: 7/10

Evochron Legacy is a single- or multiplayer sandbox iteration of the Arvoch/Starwraith franchise with a focus on PvP and conflict between the two superpowers. As a fundation it continues and expands on the great simulation aspects of earlier games and thus allows inertia battles and space combat only slightly below games like Elite:Dangerous and far above nearly all arcade space shooters.

Despite its MO-matchup the game relies on third party servers to host for this and some of these do explicitly discourage to outright forbid the PvP this game is designed around. The lack of an official server with an anything goes 24/7 guarantee is a slight limit to the game.

It does regularly get updates, small new improvements and got a major overhaul of the conquest and battle mechanics due to direct saving being a major quality of life change. This has given new life to the singleplayer aspect of the great war. This also prevents the "base respawn" bug of old in singleplayer which forced players to destroy the same enemy base twice.

There are a few things questionable in this release. For one the story even though being multifactional feels heavily focused on being done with the Alliance (based on area and progress), the push of the entire game centuries later to avoid problems with the Arvoch series leads to a "void century" problem and the technology seems to be frozen apart of the new jumpcaster wormhole technology finally on par with the Vonari from its first war centuries later.

This game is for those that enjoy space trucking, inertia battles outside of Elite:Dangerous and commanding a small battle fleet. It is also a decent game for explorers, although the things to explore are limited in their RNG value beyond the handplaced few wonders. It is definetly not friendly to completionists; the achievements are long and grindy, stay clear!

This game has my rating of fi-lay it. Play the faction war once, fight the Vonari back from a sector and build a small economic area. Maybe find your true love system and join one of the two community owned servers for a time. 

Story & Presentation: 5/10

The story is told through basic text narration quests with limited ingame animations or sequences. Quest targets are spawned in as needed and both campaigns beyond the early stage are effectively the same. This leads to the Alliance focused quest being a bit harder for Federation players. Until a while ago the Federation even when played was colored in red, showing them as the enemy of the Empire of Sol in green. This has been changed, but it did give a further feeling of the double-faction gameplay being secondary to the game's storyline.

With the story set centuries after the Dissolution war after the Mercenaries era and few wrecks telling the story back to barely one century, this game suffers a major "void century" event. While the huge genocidal war between the powers is used to explain most losses in colonies and stations, some are actually explained ingame as attacks of opportunity of the returned Vonari on the weakened powers. This is a small plus in a sea of uncertainty about what happened. Overall the player has to guess and puzzle a lot of events leading up to the "Atlas Incident".

Sadly none of the RNG systems can contain gas giants or nebula which is a major failure of the system generation. Further anomalies are handplaced in the galaxy and few if any at all. This leads to basic 1-5 planets around a sun with 1-2 asteroids. Sometimes they merge to supercluster systems up to six suns (see Eridanus in the wiki), but that is purely by chance. There are no RNG stations or settlements to discover in the void, just empty dead space.

Gameplay & Mechanics: 8/10

The gameplay already had a solid core as a space simulation with long standing inertia combat in the series and fleet management. Additional the base building was heavily expanded and atmospheric flights were given a decent overhaul. Due to recent changes to rewards for base building and fair income sources from said bases, the gameplay has become less of a diamond mine grindfest to sell to high-tech and a bit more freeform again.

The true lack of this game is the non-existent AI progress of station building/exploration/warfare. The AI won't do anything without the player and there are only two 24/7 servers online to have other players influence anything for you. 

The basic simulation of economic growth or warfare % changes will only spawn some invasions or hostiles even in deep held territory like Sierra of the Federation dropping to ALC 30% control... for no reason. It is based to deactivate the faction control drift, it has more annoyance than consequences, the AI won't wage this war. Do it yourself. 

The inactivity of the AI is the main problem of the game. It is a game tailored around being an MO, without an official server.

Visuals & Atmosphere: 7/10

The old graphics help this game run on older systems, but the planets show little visual splendor beyond single events like an aurora borealis or some nice light-locked planets in equidistance to two suns on each side. Planets will use the lightbox of the closest star otherwise, leading to 15 and 16 distance suns only being lit from the 15. 

A nice touch of the game is the use of real skyboxes. Although seeing Orion in the sky while being in a star of Orion is a bit weird. Nearby objects like planets and nebula are visible for a few sectors, suns can be seen for around 15 sectors as small light dots foreign to the skybox.

Flying over planets has a small initial charm, but due to the ever same tress being found as plants and the same bird-like creatures in the sky, after a few planets this novelty wears off. Overall the planet topography has much similarities to early No Man's Sky with basic topography either being filled with a water level or not. It's an okay experience, but nothing for an instagram story aside of the aurora borealis.

Achievements:

Not in the actual evaluation but important to note, both the military medal (grinding 1000 missions for the military or in Vonari zones) and the honor medal (getting 10000 points overall) are not friendly, entertaining or supporting completionists. [h1]Tl;dr[/h1]

You should buy it... maybe.

Burned on Elite, want something with totally different game design principles, and don't mind relearning space flight all over again? Evochron Legacy might scratch that itch if you can get over its numerous shortcomings due to being a one man dev team (albeit very skilled one man dev team). He has an unapologetic vision of what he wants in a space flight sim, but many of those decisions may confuse and frustrate you. 

And if you haven't played Elite... well, Elite costs less.

[h1]Full Review[/h1]

I really wanted to like this game after becoming too frustrated with Elite and Frontier. Unfortunately, playing it feels even more of a chore in different ways. This game was made by one person and their decades of experience in crafting a game experience shows... it's just even more niche in my opinion. I'm going to draw many comparisons to Elite below since that's where most people are going to be coming from.

- [b]Built with quality of life in mind.[/b] Elite QoL is trash. It sticks to its sim roots, both good and bad, and does not respect your time at all (engineering, anyone?). Evochron has a ton of QoL and "get to the point" gameplay decisions. With the right amount of material, you could even go across the entire universe in Evochron (using jump casters) in under an hour. Like a location, but there's no space station to dock and sell at? Build your own (even if the build system is fairly simple).

- [b]Lack of incentive to manually fly and the biggest Evochron sin.[/b] In Elite, to do basically anything you have to fly there manually. Supercruise or local space, they're still both generally manual flight short of using supercruise assist for rapid deceleration. In Evochron, the objective is to manually fly [u][i]as little as possible[/i][/u]: it's so slow compared to using your warp drive/autopilot and almost everything is on the galactic plane... you can just jump straight into most jump gates/stations barely touching the controls for minutes at a time, only bothering to manually fly to/from planets. Not much of a flight sim there if it incentivizes not actually flying.

- [b]Amount and variety of content.[/b] Elite has an unfair advantage here due to development team size. Even in Elite, there's enough variety to warrant traveling for months across the galaxy to see cool things. There are enough mission types, activities, and ships to keep you from starting to get bored for at least 100 hours (or 1000s for some people). In Evochron, there are a decent variety of mission types (arguably more interesting than Elite, but both games are lacking in areas), but most are extremely simplistic and not worth the time whatsoever. There are many ships (frames) in Evochron and the ship customization sounded REALLY fun at first... but you can figure out all of it within 5 minutes and realize how limited it is from a functional standpoint (lots of visual customization though!); you get ~5 module choices, two of which are 15-20 options on a completely linear scale, one which is 5-6 options on a linear scale, and two others are basically a 'passive skill' choice from five options. That's it.

- [b]Owning a fleet of ships... or actually just a bunch of templates.[/b] The Hanger system is [i]weird[/i] in Evochron and most players will not like it at all. In Elite, you can own as many ships as you want, specced and kitted out as you please. In Evochron, the dev goes extremely out of their way to make this as inconvenient and useless as possible. Instead of buying/storing ships, you save ship configuration "templates," sell your whole ship, buy a new one, and hope all of your old optional components (e.g. weapons) fit or else you have to sell them. If you want your old ship back, you just go into the shipyard and load the template... unless the station you're at doesn't sell that ship frame, or you're at a military carrier and it only sells military frames. It just adds this extra layer of micromanagement and does not feel fun since you're often fighting the system to get what you want done. It ultimately IS a time save if all you care about is moving up to the best ships since you sell old ships, but it lacks all of the satisfaction you get from owning a fleet. To be fair, you CAN store ships... but it clones your current ship for the full cost... what??? Why not just store the ship when you buy a new one???

- [b]Sound in space doesn't exist... but it should in games.[/b] Another objectively unfair comparison to Elite. Elite's sound design is some of the best in video games period. It adds so much weight and feedback to flight. The sound design in Evochron is... weak. It just doesn't give any real feedback in the same way. Every ship and thruster sounds the same from my experience. Weapon sounds are perfectly acceptable. This is by far the most unfair comparison on this list, but it still needed to be mentioned.

- [b]Realistic flight models aren't always more fun.[/b] A bit of a controversial opinion, but I feel most players will enjoy an Elite-like flight model more. Evochron is far and above more realistic. It is true Newtonian (or close enough). In Elite, not only does it use WW2-style physics for turning, but if you boost and turn off flight assist you will slow down after the boost... not even remotely realistic. No such thing here for Evochron. There is a hard internal cap on speed I believe, but you will never reasonably hit it. So why is Elite more fun? Trying to fly anything in Evochron feels like a leaf in the wind, even after 15 hours (mostly due to lack of Elite-style instant boost). The lacking sound design compared to Elite also doesn't help. It feels far more fun to fly when the sound design compliments what's happening and gives you feedback.

- [b]Exploration is weak when the universe is static.[/b] The universe in Evochron is much smaller than Elite... both a good and bad thing depending on who you ask. However, Elite's galaxy (or at least within each system) is in constant realistic motion in a 3-D space. Evochron is also technically 3-D, but everything is highly concentrated around the galactic ecliptic (almost everything is exactly on it). Objects in Evochron space also don't move. The map and exploration feels much closer to the X series than Elite. Due to the lack of variety mentioned above, there's also very little reason to explore in Evochron. Sure... you could establish new trade routes by building stations, colonize more of uncharted space, or discover cool looking things... but why? There's no reason to do any of it. Other than 2-3 necessary secrets off the beaten path for progression, it's much easier to do everything in charted space. However, one pro for Evochron is fully atmospheric planets with weather, water, sparse vegetation, and even aurora... way more interesting than Elite's planets.

- [b]Does it run on a toaster?[/b] The one thing I will not complain about is the visual fidelity of the game. One man show, remember? The dev has maintained their visual style for years (decades, really) and it has given the entire series an identity. I actually like it quite a bit despite the overall lower quality (the planet accretion disk textures though...). But one major negative is the game's optimization which I believe is more of a limitation of the game engine rather than lack of dev skill. In short, on my rig (13600k, RTX 3080 at 1440p/144fps), Elite on high/ultra settings runs far better than Evochron on high settings. It's very rare for me to get frame drops in Elite and not be able to see where the bottleneck is based on sensor readouts (excluding some obvious Odyssey content). In Evochron, I'll drop frames with the GPU usage under 30%, CPU usage under 30% (both entire package and max single core usage), plenty of fast RAM available, and a good NVMe SSD. I saw similar performance issues with a completely different system as well (6700k, GTX 1080 at 1080p).

This game gets a hard recommend from me. Lots of reasons why.

There are very few full-featured VR+HOTAS capable space sims out there. The most obvious alternative is Elite Dangerous,  which I played for over 250 hours, and would've happily continued playing had the devs of Elite not put VR on life support. Unfortunately over my two years with Elite and it's updates, performance in VR had gotten worse to the point where I was no longer having fun in game and instead constantly fighting optimization issues despite having upgraded to an RTX 3070 during that time. In addition, it was clear they had no intention of supporting VR for the new content they were introducing. And at 250 hours in, new content was sorely needed.

It was time to find something new. A really bitter pill to swallow as over the pandemic I LIVED inside my ship, I had become so incredibly attached to my amazing time with Elite in VR. With Star Citizen lacking VR support (and just general content) I really didn't think I would ever experience anything quite like Elite in VR again. I looked and searched for something which would engross me in the same way Elite did in the beginning, but couldn't find what I was looking for, and my HOTAS and Headset went into the cupboard and began collecting dust. 

And then, through sheer chance, I find this game nearly 2 years later while randomly browsing steam. How the ♥♥♥♥ did I miss this game before? On paper this game had it all, VR support, HOTAS support, and the full space sim experience. Comparisons to Elite were rife on forums and reviews the internet over. This was it! It was time to dive in. 

But before I discuss what makes Evochron great, a special mention needs to be called out to it's developer who frankly has given me one of the best customer service experiences I have ever encountered. Without boring with the details, I had a simple tracking issue in VR which prevented me from playing without extreme motion sickness - it required a game update to fix. A mention of it on the steam forums and within the space of 24 hours my specific issue was resolved. In addition, when I made an additional feature request off the back of that fix, that TOO was delivered within 24 hours. All of this despite the game not having VR support in the "official" sense. (It has to be set up by enabling an option and editing some txt files rather than be a "plug and play" experience)

This guy has complete and utter dedication to his product and the community. Just check out the forums for yourself and see the engagement. That alone is in such stark contrast to the attitudes of Frontier (Elite Devs) that it instantly elevates this game to legendary status, and ensures I will be speaking about (and hopefully playing!) Evochron Legacy for a long time to come.

So this game fills a great niche, and has a passionate dev, but what actually makes it great? To be clear, this game is absolutely not Elite. Nor is it trying to be. In fact I would go as far as to say that this game is everything Elite ISN'T. Which depending on what you're looking from a VR+HOTAS space sim might be the refreshing change up you need.

To put it simply, where Elite has style, Evochron Legacy has substance. 

Evochron Legacy is an immensely deep game with lots of interconnecting systems that come together to give the player a level of freedom and agency which is not present in Elite.

Yes I miss the slick graphics and sound design of Elite, the noises and atmosphere of a busy space station in Elite are second to none. But in Elite the illusion of immersion is shattered the moment you look towards the painted-on texture of an earth like planet knowing you cannot land there, or as you fly out to the edges of a solar system to discover its invisible walls. Or the moment you realize the carrier you've been grinding for is basically just a menu screen with extra steps. Every corner of Elites systems have grind or limitations reminding the player that they cannot do things in the way they want or expect.

Evochron is the opposite of that in a lot of ways. It puts features and player freedom and agency above all else. The graphics are deceptive as they lead you to believe this game is simple or bereft of detail, but that couldn't be further from the truth. Every aspect of this game has been crafted to ALLOW the player instead of restrict them (within reason). Features such as being able to actually fly through the atmosphere of every planet (including gas giants!) and have the atmosphere actually effect the ship flight model, being able build bases both in space and on land, have an actual effect on the economy, build and design ships from the ground up, Fly anywhere seamlessly, and switch up loadouts and play-styles completely at a whim. 

If you point your nose towards something in Evochron and dig deeper, you'll likely discover some new detail or aspect or feature which pleasantly surprises. Like how I wanted to check out a planet and while cruising around close to the ground I saw birds. BIRDS, IN A SPACE GAME. Sure they were janky looking but at least they were THERE. At this stage I'd take that over the vaporware promises of Elite and Star Citizen. 

Unfortunately, there are obvious areas which have to be sacrificed when you're a one man dev on a mission to develop these deep and complex games. Not everyone is Roberts Space Industries and nor do they want to be. 

The sound and graphics in this game can be wildly inconsistent ranging from beautiful to downright ugly. Particularly on planets the game takes on an almost retro PS2 style charm. And the tutorial took me three evening of gaming time to fully complete and grasp. This game is HARDCORE and there's a lot here in first impressions which could put people off. If you stick it out and look past that, you'll find plenty in this game which will blow your mind. I think it speaks volumes that even though this game is as rough around the edges as it is - particularly for new players - I still want to experience all of what it has to offer because this game offers depth and is begging to be explored.

I like deep and complex games, I'm not afraid to learn how to play them. I also love space and space sim games. To find a space sim game of this depth and complexity, in VR, with HOTAS support, and with a dev that actually gives a ♥♥♥♥. There is nothing else. It simply doesn't exist.

This game is spectacular. While Elite: Dangerous continues to spiral down into a garbage fire (just kidding, Elite is cool), I went out in search of a new space sim and holy crap, I found it.

While this may not be the best looking game out there, this game has so much to offer that completely makes up for it (assuming you're someone who really cares about graphics). It's quite incredible, especially considering the fact that this game was made and is maintained by ONE GUY. The fact that he does this in his free time and is still pushing out updates is incredible. Big ups to the developer. There is just so much that you can do in this game. You can take contracts, build bases, trade, mine, shoot stuff, play online, play offline, go exploring, and probably tons of other stuff that I haven't found yet.

There is also a lot of customization when it comes to your ship. You can kit your ship out however you want and for whatever task you might be trying to accomplish. While there's a lot you can customize, it's still pretty easy to follow along with and understand what you're doing. I hate when space games make the customization super in-depth to where you can't really understand what changing something will affect on your ship.

The flying in this game is amazing. The model itself is certainly better than similar games (Elite). It feels a lot less arcade-y and a lot more what you would think flying a spaceship should feel like. There's no "space breaks" or turning rate limits. You can go as fast as you want. If you completely turn off your inertial dampening system (IDS in-game) you can get spinning so fast that you literally tear your ship apart and blow up lol.

Probably the biggest draw to this game is the community. Unfortunately it is small, since this game has been out for so long, but the people that do still play this game are super friendly and inviting. I've only been playing for a couple weeks and already feel like I'm "part of the crew." Of course, you don't have to play in multiplayer, like I said above, but I think it makes the game a lot more fun to do missions with other pilots. You can also host your own server, or connect directly with IP to play with friends. The game is really versatile when it comes to how you can play this game with other people.

A couple other things to mention, you can play this game in VR (which looks amazing), you can play with a HOTAS or HOSAS setup (pretty much anything will work from my experience) and a player made a Voice Attack pack that is absolutely amazing and completely changes the way you play the game. The game also appears to be extremely moddable, though I haven't dabbled much with mods yet. You seem to also be able to write your own quests and share them with friends, which is super cool.

To summarize, this is probably my favorite space sim. It's simply wonderful how much stuff you can do. If you're a fan of space sims, check this game out and come play with us!

2) The missions are varied and go beyond the usual "fly passenger here, or deliver x material here". You still get these but they're in between some greats. I have been playing StarWraith games since Evochron Mercenary. There were two games prior which I didnt try because the subject matter overlaps and they were older. These are the efforts of one man to produce his vision of the best space sim sandbox and I think he has succeeded.

I bought mercenary because of the non-military content such as exploration and mining. While I had no intention of doing the combat stuff, my explorations took me into places that were involved in a war and no matter how hard you try to stay out of a bar room brawl, someone is going to take a swing at you eventually.

While the space appears limited, it is in fact expansive. Looking at the map does not reveal all. There is exploring to do. Things out there need finding from wrecks and stations all the way up to planets! There are resources to harvest in space and on the planets and to trade both on planetary cites and stations near planets. There are quest chains and individual missions. You can build your own stations and manufacturing facilities. There is a straight forward economy that you can view and manipulate and a very active NPC population. 

You can embark on a term of military service in one of the war zones which generate their own missions. While I dont play these types of games for the combat.. I will say that the combat in this game is addictive. 

With all that being said this is not a simplistic sim. The tutorial is better than in most of these types of games and I would say you need at least 3-4 hours in the game before you start getting comfortable. The flight model employs a good dose of Newtonian Physics and requires your attention. Planetary re-entry likewise requires you to pay attention to speed and altitude so you dont  burn up when you hit the atmosphere. 

I have not explored ALL the game has to offer but I doubt you can explore all of space and find all the things in it. There is also "Riftspace" and the places it will lead you to but that is for you to find.

TL;DR: Eurotruck Simulator dans l'espace. Mieux codé, mais vraiment ne vous attendez pas à du fun en barres, c'est un jeu pour passer le temps.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Historique[/h2]

J'ai longuement joué à Evochron Mercenary, hors Steam. Je l'ai entièrement traduit pour les (rares) francophones qui en avaient besoin. J'ai réécrit le Technical Flight Manual créé par un fan, qui donne des informations étendues sur tous les aspects de l'univers, des vaisseaux aux technologies employées… J'ai même écrit un outil de triangulation en Javascript pour trouver les planètes cachées.

Alors est-ce que je recommande Evochron Legacy ? Bien sûr. Mais il faut comprendre une chose : c'est développé par un seul homme, dans son coin.

[h2]Le rêve d'un seul homme, le cauchemar de milliers d'autres[/h2]

Le côté positif, c'est que comme il est très à l'écoute et qu'il fait ses jeux depuis des décennies, il y a de très nombreuses fonctionnalités et très, très peu de bugs. Pour vous donner une idée, si vous vous trouvez à court de carburant dans un secteur isolé et que vous demandez de l'aide à Vice, il vous offrira de vous replacer à un secteur paisible en lui envoyant votre sauvegarde. C'est le genre de développeur qui joue à ses jeux, et ça se ressent. Atterrissage sur les planètes avant Elite: Dangerous, nombreux types de contrats, création de votre propre vaisseau (en choisissant sa forme et ses composants), construction de stations et de villes, deux factions et une race hostile, courses de vaisseaux, multiples carrières possibles (du simple mineur au pilote de combat donnant des ordres à sa flotte), recrutement de membres d'équipage, objets cachés, et j'en passe. Il y a tout ce que les autres ne font qu'à moitié. Eh, à part Elite, il y a peu de jeux qui vous permettent de configurer des raccourcis de manettes : quasiment toutes les commandes tiennent sur un contrôleur XBOX 360 si on le configure correctement.

Le côté négatif, c'est aussi que ce n'est développé que par un seul homme. Les graphismes sont, on ne va pas se le cacher, assez moches (même si l'on voit l'amélioration au fil des itérations de la série). Le HUD de base est très encombré quand on le compare aux trois grands du genre que sont Elite: Dangerous, Star Citizen et la série X, ce qui offre une UI horrible. Les sons sont un poil meilleurs que ceux que l'on retrouve dans les jeux gratuits à la Oolite, mais les mouvements de caméra y sont les mêmes : inexistants. Ce qui fait que la sensation du pilotage pourrait être grandement meilleure : c'est un réel plaisir de faire des manœuvres dans le vide en sortie de station dans Elite, et c'est juste fade dans Evochron. Ce développeur brille plus par son code que par le reste, il faut bien avouer.

Vice ne peut se permettre d'avoir une communauté plus large, et pourtant c'est bien de cela dont il a besoin. Il y a deux-trois serveurs qui se battent en duel, mais c'est suffisant pour le nombre de joueurs. Non, je parle plus des mods. Parce que oui, tout ou presque est modable dans Evochron. Du HUD à la texture des planètes, de la police d'affichage aux vaisseaux et cockpits. Vice fournit même tous les outils nécessaires. Le souci de la taille de la communauté joue alors un rôle important : le nombre de mods est très, très limité. Vous voulez augmenter la résolution des textures ? Il n'y a qu'un mod pour cela. Changer les sons ? Il y en a deux, maximum. La musique ? Un seul. Même pour le HUD vous n'en trouverez pas plus de trois encore fonctionnels. Et pour tout ce qui est des modèles 3D des divers objets et cockpits, il n'y en a pas. Ah si, un pour les arbres. Youhou.

J'ai donc passé plusieurs jours à créer mon HUD minimaliste, avec son UI aux petits oignons, et j'en ressors avec cette impression : il y a tout pour aller taquiner les grands au niveau du code, il manque sans doute des mouvements de caméra pour que l'on [i]sente[/i] que l'on pilote un vaisseau. Mais pour le reste, c'est un jeu à construire soi-même. Avec de meilleurs assets et une meilleure UI, on aurait une véritable pépite à la Helium Rain, la communauté et les fonctionnalités en plus.

[h2]Monotonie : à comparer avec Mercenary[/h2]

En 50 heures, j'ai le meilleur vaisseau possible, la seule carotte pour me faire avancer ce sont mes rangs de réputation, et il est peu probable que je cherche à les grind tellement ce serait long et monotone (j'aurais plus vite fait de me trouver un second boulot). Un rapide calcul me fait comprendre pourquoi moins de 0,5 % des joueurs ont les succès Steam. Au train où je vais, il me faudrait 500 heures pour terminer les rangs en civil, et probablement autant pour les rangs militaires. La monotonie est présente.

Le système de factions a été simplifié depuis Mercenary : on est passé d'une dizaine de factions à… deux. Là, dans l'état des choses, ça ne fonctionne pas : je traverse un système à 29 % d'occupation alliée, je vaque à mes occupations, et quand je reviens il est tombé à 7 %. Et c'est un système en plein centre de la zone de ma faction ! L'ennemi arrive et progresse, il ne prend aucune station ou quoi que ce soit, juste sa barre de progression se remplit jusqu'au moment où elle est assez pleine pour que l'on voit popper des vaisseaux hostiles un peu partout. Et vous savez quoi ? On ne peut rien faire pour l'en empêcher. Les stations sont censées offrir des contrats de combat, mais en 50 heures je n'en ai vu aucun, même dans les zones disputées. Au moins dans Mercenary, on avait ce genre de contrats pratiquement à chaque station vu que tout le monde était en guerre contre son voisin, il y avait moyen de faire bouger un peu les lignes, ça faisait monter notre rang militaire, et changeait de la routine. Donc vous en êtes réduits à faire les contrats civils proposés aux stations, on en a fait le tour en quelques heures. Il y a de belles trouvailles, des trucs funs à faire une fois ou deux, mais les contrats ne changent rien, ils ajoutent simplement 1 point à votre rang civil (sur 1000 !), et à peine plus d'argent que ce que vous ramasseriez en vous baissant dans un couloir. Je ne vois pas comment on peut passer 500 heures sur ce titre, très sincèrement. C'est frustrant : ce space sim a toutes les fonctionnalités des autres réunis, mais il est aussi très, très vide, et une fois passée la découverte des premières heures, sans aucune saveur. Il n'y a aucune sensation d'accomplissement. Hourra ! j'ai passé le rang Compétent, je vais gagner 2 % de plus sur la misère que me rapporteront les 300 contrats supplémentaires que j'ai à effectuer pour atteindre le rang suivant…

Si j'ai tenu 50 h, c'est simplement parce que j'avais besoin cette semaine d'une activité vide de sens, de manière thérapeutique, et que pour faire le plein c'est mieux de se balader dans une nébuleuse que sur une aire d'autoroute.

[h2]Verdict[/h2] 

C'est donc avec une certaine amertume que je recommande ce titre, en sachant qu'il est un potentiel gâché. Ce sera sans doute le dernier StarWraith que j'achèterais. Ce jeu souffre de la dette technique accumulée depuis les débuts de la série. Vice en est conscient, mais il y a peu de chances qu'il refonde entièrement le jeu, ce dont il aurait besoin pour attirer de nouveaux joueurs. 

Si vous n'avez pas peur des graphismes dépassés, foncez.

Si vous voulez un Eurotruck Simulator dans l'espace, moins cher et plus brut de décoffrage qu'Elite, avec la même absence de réflexion sur l'UI et la QOL qu'Eurotruck, allez-y.

Si vous êtes du genre à faire vos propres packs de texture Minecraft parce que la base c'est bien mais ce serait quand même mieux que les champs de blé soient animés en donnant l'impression d'une douce brise, allez-y, vous aurez amplement cette satisfaction. 

Mais ne l'achetez pas si vous vous dites « de toute façon je trouverai bien un mod », la réponse est non.
